name: Karakalpak
variety: Literary Karakalpak of Karakalpakstan (Uzbekistan), based on the north-eastern dialect; Latin script (Cyrillic also in use)
sources: Menges, Karl H. (1947). Qaraqałpaq Grammar. Part One: Phonology. King's Crown Press.
Kirchner, Mark (1998). Kazakh and Karakalpak. In Lars Johanson & Éva Á. Csató (eds.), The Turkic Languages. Routledge.
contrasts: nine vowels: front /i y e ø æ/ (i ú e ó á) and back /ɯ u o ɑ/ (ı u o a)
velar /k ɡ/ versus uvular /q ʁ/, tied to vowel backness in native words
sibilant shift typical of the Kipchak-Nogai group: /ʃ/ where most Turkic languages have /tʃ/ and /s/ where they have /ʃ/ (úsh 'three', bes 'five', tas 'stone')
allophony: k and g are velar next to front vowels; q and ǵ [ʁ] occur next to back vowels
word-initial /e/ has a palatal on-glide [je] and word-initial /o ø/ a labial on-glide [wo wø], as in Kazakh
the high vowels are short and lax and may be dropped in fast speech
/l/ is velarised next to back vowels
suffix-initial consonants assimilate to the end of the stem (plural -lar, -ler; ablative -dan, -tan, -nan)
/f v ts tʃ/ occur in loanwords only; /h/ and /x/ occur mainly in Arabic and Persian loans
phonotactics: no onset clusters in native words
coda clusters are sonorant + obstruent (tórt, qırq)
backness harmony in native words and suffixes; rounding harmony is weak and is not written beyond the first syllable
Russian and other loans may break harmony

stress.type: fixed final by default, with morphological exceptions
stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word; predicative personal endings, the negative suffix and the question particle are unstressed and leave the stress on the syllable before them.
stress.cues: not instrumentally studied in the sources used

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: high vowels are short and may be dropped between consonants; other vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: Low confidence: no instrumental study of Karakalpak timing was available to me.

length.notes: No vowel length contrast. Geminates occur at morpheme boundaries and in a few stems.

intonation.declarative: rise at the end of non-final phrases, fall at the end of the statement
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the particle ma/me (ba/be, pa/pe); pitch is high before the particle or rises on it
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: rise to a high on the final stressed syllable
intonation.notes: Low confidence: no instrumental study of Karakalpak intonation was available to me; the entries follow the general pattern of the better described Turkic languages (Turkish, Kazakh).

problems: no stress rule is set for kaa, so the default penultimate stress applies (bala, kitaplar, úyler are stressed before the last syllable); Karakalpak stress is final
ı is the schwa phoneme @, which eSpeak cannot stress: words whose only vowel is ı get no stress at all (qız, mıń, jıldız)
the phoneme table is a copy of the Kazakh one; the mid vowel ó (/ø/) has the short duration of the high vowels (100 against 200)
every l that does not stand directly before a front vowel is dark [ɫ], also in front-vowel words (el, bel, kel-)
the apostrophe-like letter ʼ that replaces Cyrillic ь and ъ has no rule
no labial on-glide for word-initial o and ó
unstressable suffixes and particles are not handled
t is the unaspirated base2 stop while p and k use aspirated samples
good: Latin and Cyrillic spelling are both accepted
all nine vowels are present; q, ǵ, ń are [q], [ʁ], [ŋ]
vowel harmony follows from the spelling

notes: The consonant list includes /f v ts tʃ/, which occur in loanwords only. The degree of aspiration of the voiceless stops is not documented in the sources used.
